subject: Copywriting
title: Rosie the Riveter
description: Learn Rosie the Riveter in one minute.

hook.text: 'We Can Do It!' Rosie the Riveter was a propaganda poster designed to recruit women into wartime factories.

buildup.text: J. Howard Miller designed the poster for Westinghouse in 1943.

discovery.text: Six million women entered the workforce during WWII.

twist.text: After the war, new propaganda told women to return home. The same tools that liberated were used to re-confine.

climax.text: Rosie proves propaganda can reshape identity. 'We Can Do It!' didn't just sell a job—it redefined who women could be.

punchline.text: Two weeks on display. 80 years of cultural impact. Copy reshapes identity.

quiz.question: How long was the original Rosie the Riveter poster displayed?

details.summary: Rosie the Riveter became the iconic symbol of American women's wartime labor during World War II. Originally a government propaganda campaign to recruit women into factories, Rosie transcended her origins to become an enduring feminist icon — proof that propaganda can outlive its original purpose.
details.whyItMatters: Rosie demonstrates how propaganda imagery can take on a life of its own. Understanding this phenomenon helps communicators appreciate that once released into culture, messages evolve beyond the creator's intent.
takeaways: Rosie was created as government propaganda to fill wartime labor shortages
The 'We Can Do It!' poster became a feminist icon decades later
Propaganda symbols can be repurposed by new movements for new meanings

faq.question: Was Rosie the Riveter based on a real person?
faq.answer: The character was a composite, though several real women have been identified as inspirations. The famous 'We Can Do It!' poster by J. Howard Miller was actually displayed for only two weeks in a Westinghouse factory before being forgotten and rediscovered decades later.

faq.question: How did Rosie become a feminist symbol?
faq.answer: In the 1980s, feminists rediscovered the 'We Can Do It!' poster and adopted it as a symbol of female empowerment. Its original purpose — recruiting women for temporary wartime work — was replaced by a broader message of permanent female capability and strength.
